newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Heads on block in France's GAN row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Heads on block in France's GAN row.

text.p: The French government called on the head of state insurer GAN to resign on Monday after abandoning a tender to privatise GAN's banking subsidiary CIC and criticising the chairmen of both groups for failing to promote the sell-off.

The government's wrath over the privatisation failure looked set to claim two heads at once -- those of GAN chairman Jean-Jacques Bonnaud and of Bernard Yoncourt, chairman of its profitable regional banking subsidiary Credit Industriel et Commercial (CIC),
"The government has asked for the resignation of Mr Jean-Jacques Bonnaud," a finance ministry spokeswoman said.

A source close to the case said the new GAN chairman would then name a new boss at CIC but declined to give any names, saying only that Bonnaud's replacement could be made known by the end of the week.
"The new chairman of GAN will name a new head of CIC," the source said.
Neither GAN (Groupe des Assurances Nationales) nor CIC would make any immediate comment in the wake of the news.
Yoncourt infuriated Finance Minister Jean Arthuis in October after declaring on television that the sale of CIC to a major French bank could spell "death" for the banking group.

Arthuis said at the time he would "draw the consequences" of Yoncourt's "unacceptable" behaviour and made it clear last week when announcing the cancellation of the CIC privatisation tender that Bonnaud, who is ultimately responsible for CIC as part of the GAN group, was also in the firing line.
"The managers of GAN and CIC did not behave in a way to encouarge progress in this process," he said last week.
The government received only two bids for CIC, a grouping of 11 regional banks whose clients are mainly big and medium sized companies -- from Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP) and Societe Generale.

The French privatisation commission rejected the offer from Societe Generale on the grounds it did not comply with the terms imposed by the government, of which the most important is that any buyer must preserve the bank's regional integrity.
Arthuis said he was determined to privatise the group but that he was breaking off a tender in which there was only one eligible offer on the table to take more time to reflect.
Staff and trade unions opposed the sell-off with strikes and protests over feared job losses but the spectre of a break-up of the group also sparked widespread fears among local politicians.
The government's options appear limited as long as it sticks to the strict conditions for all potential buyers.

But two possibilities suggested by banking analysts and the media after the privatisation tender was cancelled are a re-run in which the savings bank group Caisse d'Epargne could also enter the bidding and some form of coordinated takeover of each of the 11 regional banks which would keep the grouping intact.

CIC has a value of around 14 billion francs ($2.7 billion) on GAN's books, which would correspond to about 9.4 billion francs for the 67 percent which the government had offered for sale in the now defunct tender.

Many investment analysts believe the government's insistence on conditions which also include preserving a pact on the sale of GAN insurance via CIC branches will keep offer prices low. ($=5.0955 french francs)
